title: Your Job Rights: Pay, Contract and Harassment
summary: Appointment letter, notice period, unpaid salary, harassment at work, PF and gratuity.
sectionRefs: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013

body.text: If you work, you must be paid. On time, and in full. The law also protects you on your contract, notice, leave and harassment. If you know the basics, you can act instead of worry.
Your appointment letter and your contract

items: Read your appointment letter. It says your salary, work hours, notice period, leave and when the job can end.
Keep a signed copy. If someone promises you something by word of mouth, ask them to write it down.
Money can be cut from your pay only if the law allows it. If it is cut for no reason, you can complain to the labour office.
Your pay must come on the agreed date. For many workers, within 7 to 10 days after the pay period ends.
Keep your payslips and bank statements. They show how much was owed and how much was paid.
Your employer cannot hold back your full and final settlement (the last payment of all your dues) without a lawful reason.

body.text: Notice, resignation and losing the job

items: A notice period is the time your contract or the law says you must give before leaving. Both sides should respect it.
You can resign. Your employer must still pay you for the days you worked.
If your job is ended, it must follow the contract and the law. If you are sacked to take revenge for a complaint, you can challenge it.
Leave is decided by your contract and the labour law that applies to you.
Sexual harassment at work is not allowed. Workplaces with enough staff must have an Internal Committee (a group that looks into such complaints).
You can complain to the Internal Committee. In small workplaces, you can complain to the Local Committee.
Provident Fund (PF) is a savings fund for your retirement. In covered workplaces, your employer must pay into it.
Gratuity (a lump sum your employer pays you) is usually paid after five years of continuous service, in covered cases.
ESI (medical cover) and other benefits apply where your workplace is covered.

body.text: Never sign a resignation or settlement letter you do not understand. Signing it may reduce what you can claim.
Keep your appointment letter, payslips, attendance records, bank statements and any written promises. These are your proof.
If your salary is not paid, you can complain to the Labour Commissioner or apply to recover the money owed to you. For PF problems, complain to the EPFO.

practicalSteps: Collect your appointment letter, payslips, attendance records and bank statements.
Send a polite written request for your money. Keep a copy.
File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner or the labour court.
For PF problems, complain to the EPFO. For harassment, go to the Internal or Local Committee.
For unpaid salary, you can file an application to recover the money owed to you.
exceptions: Some kinds of workers, and very small workplaces, follow different limits under the law.
Some people who earn more may not be covered by parts of the wage laws. But their contract and the general law still apply.

faqs.q: Can my employer cut my salary as a punishment?
faqs.a: Money can be cut only when the law allows it. If pay is cut as punishment with no legal reason, you can complain to the labour office.

faqs.q: What about my PF and gratuity?
faqs.a: In covered workplaces, your employer must pay into your PF. Gratuity is paid after five years of continuous service in covered cases.

misconceptions.myth: If I complain, I will surely lose my job.
misconceptions.fact: Punishing you for complaining is against the law. You can complain to the labour office. Free legal aid services and workers' unions can help you.
